# Dangerous liaisons: social AI and the problem with the relational turn to moral status

- Open Forum
- Open access
- Published: 22 October 2025

- Adrienne de Ruiter 1 

## Abstract

The question what moral status to ascribe to artificially intelligent entities, such as social robots, is at the forefront of academic debate. The related question as to how social AI affects the moral status we can ascribe to ourselves as human beings, by contrast, has received far less attention. Philosophers who discuss this issue propose a relational turn: human moral status should not be understood to be based on uniquely or typically human traits or capacities but derives from interpersonal interactions and practices through which people come to respect and morally value others. The aim of this article is to set out how developments in the field of social AI pose a problem not only to traits-based accounts of (human) moral status, but also to the relational approach. Our ways of morally relating to others are often mistaken and social AI heightens this risk, as it is purposefully designed to evoke moral responses in humans by displaying traits and mirroring forms of interaction that we would ascribe moral relevance in relations with fellow humans or (non-human) animals. If we cannot take the moral appearance of interactions with social AI at face value, we need further normative grounds to distinguish relations in which moral status is properly ascribed from those where it is not.

## 1 Introduction

Accounting for moral status has never been easy. Yet, with the rise of social AI and robotics, matters have become decidedly more difficult. Philosophers in the field of ethics of technology have argued that social AI challenges traits based accounts of moral status that claim that people, as well as other beings and entities, deserve moral respect or consideration due to particular features or capacities, such as rationality, personhood or sentience (see, e.g. Coeckelbergh 2012, 2023; Gunkel 2007, 2016, 2022). With the rise of social AI, establishing what traits are morally relevant, what these traits entail and how we can know who or what possesses them becomes even more complicated (Coeckelbergh 2012; Gunkel 2016). As an alternative, these scholars propose taking a relational turn, which entails that moral status should not be grounded in traits or capacities of beings and entities but understood to be socially constituted through interactions. This alternative allows for a more open attitude towards the moral importance that artificial entities may take on in a changing social world in which people develop meaningful relations with social AI and reflects the idea that what we care about matters morally.

The aim of this article is to set out how developments in the field of social AI not only present a problem for traits based accounts of moral status, as correctly identified by proponents of the relational turn, but pose fundamental challenges to this relational approach as well. Our ways of relating to others are often mistaken, and social AI deepens this risk, as it is purposefully designed to evoke moral responses in humans by displaying traits and mirroring forms of interaction that we would ascribe moral value in relations with fellow human beings and (non-human) animals. If we cannot take the moral appearance of relations with social AI at face value, we need further normative grounds to distinguish relations in which moral status is properly ascribed from those where it is not. My proposal is to consider the vulnerabilities of various kinds of beings and entities as leading in determining their moral status, casting moral status fundamentally as a form of protection against preventable suffering. This article thereby seeks to offer an alternative understanding of moral status in light of current technological developments, which warns against expanding our moral circle to include social AI and robots at the current point of technological development.

The first part of this article provides an overview of debates in the field of philosophy and ethics of technology about the moral status of social robots and AI. The second part discusses the work of Mark Coeckelbergh and David Gunkel as the main proponents of the relational turn. The third part identifies key issues that social AI and robotics pose to the relational view of moral status. The fourth part argues for an alternative approach that grounds moral status in the notion of distinct webs of vulnerabilities to suffering that characterise particular modes of being. The conclusion brings the main lines of argument together and considers the moral and practical implications of the proposed alternative.

## 2 Accounting for (human) moral status in the ethics of technology

With rapid advances taking place in the field of (social) AI and robotics in recent years, scholars have shown increasing interest in the moral questions raised by these technologies (see, e.g. Bartneck et al. 2021; Coeckelbergh 2020; Dubber et al. 2020; Liao 2020; Lin et al. 2020; Nyholm 2020; Véliz 2024; Von Braun et al. 2021). Many scholars have explored our relation to (social) AI, for example, by examining how human virtuous conduct is impacted through interactions with (social) AI (see, e.g. Cappuccio et al. 2021; Danaher 2019; de Graaf 2016; Elder 2017; Farina et al. 2024; Sparrow 2021; Vallor 2016) or by elaborating ways to build (social) AI in responsible ways (see, e.g. Dignum 2019; Floridi et al. 2021; Hagendorff 2020; Jobin et al. 2019; Mittelstadt 2019; Russell 2019; Shneiderman 2022). Several studies also consider what moral status we should ascribe to (social) AI and robots given the expanding capacities of these technologies and the interactions we can entertain with them (see, e.g. Coeckelbergh 2010; Danaher 2020; Gibert and Martin 2022; Gordon 2020; Gunkel 2012, 2018; Harris and Anthis 2021; Himma 2009; Mosakas 2021; Sullins 2011; Tavani 2018; Torrance 2014). Footnote 1 

This literature identifies various traits and capacities as central to determining the moral status of social AI and robotics. These traits and capacities include consciousness (Andreotta 2021; Basl 2014; Mosakas 2021; Risse 2019; Torrance 2014; Turner 2019), self-awareness (Cave et al. 2018), sentience (Gibert and Martin 2022; Smids 2020) and moral reasoning and decision-making (Gordon 2020). Other authors contend that moral status depends on the capacity of social AI and robots to behave in ways akin to the conduct of beings and entities that hold moral status (Danaher 2020). A further approach argues that moral status derives from the interactions between humans and social AI and robotics, rather than from traits, capacities or performances (Coeckelbergh 2012, 2023; Gunkel 2007, 2016, 2022).

While a growing body of literature addresses the question of the moral status of social AI and robots, relatively little attention has been paid to the impact of these technologies on the moral status of human beings. This lack of attention is surprising, as the rise of social artificial entities is prone to affect our thinking about human moral status. Moral status is a partially hierarchical notion, which entails that people maintain that certain groups of beings or entities hold a particular standing relative to other groups of beings or entities (Clarke and Savulescu 2021). According to this hierarchical mode of reasoning, it is often believed that humans hold a moral status that is higher than the moral status of non-human animals. This hierarchical mode of reasoning also works on a more fine-grained level, as may be seen reflected, for example, in the fact that the moral status of wolves is generally held to be higher than that of goldfish.

Human moral status is pivotal to this hierarchy, as it anchors many other forms of moral status in the sense that the moral status of other beings and entities is often assessed in comparison to human traits, capacities and modes of relating. This centrality of the human in our thinking about moral status is assumed to rely not simply on the fact that we, as the attributers of moral status, are humans (see, e.g. Kagan 2016). Many philosophers believe that the high moral status we ascribe to human beings is deserved, based on particular traits or capacities that humans (generally) possess or the kind of relations that we can entertain with fellow human beings (see, e.g. Clarke and Savulescu 2021; Gewirth 1992; Kagan 2016; Waldron 2017; Warren 1997).

Anchoring the ascription of moral status in human traits and relationality means, however, that our reasoning about moral status can be destabilised if new entities enter our social sphere, which possess traits or capacities that we hold to be morally relevant in humans or can engage in social interactions with humans in ways that feel akin or perhaps even more meaningful to us than the relations we maintain with people. Since rapid advances are being made in the field of social AI and robotics in mirroring both traits and modes of relationality that we value in human beings, these technologies are due to influence our thinking about the moral status we hold as people. Considering how developments in social AI and robotics affect our views of human moral status is therefore crucial.

## 3 Taking a relational turn

Influential work on the impact of social AI and robotics on the moral status of human beings has been carried out by the philosophers Mark Coeckelbergh (2012, 2023) and David Gunkel (2007, 2016, 2022). Both the authors critique traits based accounts of human moral status. Traits-based accounts maintain that certain uniquely or typically human qualities, such as rationality or autonomous agency, or the ability to develop these, grant a special standing to people in contrast to non-human animals or objects. As Luciano Floridi notes, on this account, ‘what the entity is determines the degree of moral value it enjoys, if any’ (2013, 116). What an entity ‘is’ is decided by the relevant moral traits it possesses. The centrality of traits based accounts in philosophy and ethics can be seen reflected in the fact that even attempts to ground the moral status of non-human animals tend to take the traits of humans as a reference point. In this way, central arguments for animal moral status signal similarities in life or sentience between human and non-human animals (cf. Regan 1983/ 2016; Singer 1975) to justify the attribution of a (higher) moral status to non-human animals.

Coeckelbergh and Gunkel criticise traits based approaches to human moral status, pointing to disagreement about which traits, if any, can ground human moral status, dissensus about what these traits entail and epistemic uncertainty about whether others possess these traits. Gunkel thus notes that taking into account the history of traits based justifications for human moral status shows that ‘many properties that at one time seemed both necessary and sufficient have turned out to be spurious, prejudicial or both’ (2016, 199). Properties thought to justify a high moral standing often served the interests of dominant groups in society, ruling out equal moral consideration of women, people of different races, ethnicities, or nationality, or other persons considered of low social standing. This historical record emphasises the need to look critically at the properties we deem central to moral status. In the case of social AI and robotics, it is particularly relevant to guard against unjustified exclusions from moral consideration through potential biases against what is inanimate rather than alive, engineered rather than born and artificial rather than natural, or against hybrid forms of existence that dispel these dichotomic oppositions (Floridi 2013, 64).
